svg.text: Each request keeps its own simple function. A separate task answers all waiting calls with one query.
for (id, row) in pair(batch, rows) { send(id, row) }

g.text: A request arrives and its handler runs like any other function.
It needs one user, so it calls users.call(key).
call() registers a reply slot under a new id, then puts only the key and the id in the queue.
.await parks the handler on its slot. No thread is blocked: it runs #2 and #3, which do the same.
A separate batcher task takes every call that is waiting right now: three keys.
It does not wait for more. Whoever is in the queue at this moment goes into the batch.
One query for all three keys: … WHERE path = ANY('{u17,u42,u99}').
Postgres answers with three rows in one round trip instead of three.
Each row is matched to its call by key and sent to the reply slot with that call's id.
Sending into the slot wakes the handler that is parked on it. The slot is used up.
The handler continues right after .await, with its own row in user.
From its point of view, users.call(key) simply returned Ada.

svg.text: Simplified pseudocode. In mq-bridge, Caller::call is the handler side; the batcher is a route with a lookup middleware.
